Buffett Hands Berkshire Chairman’s Seat to Son Howard
 
Plus, Coinbase shares soar and Bank of Japan’s rate hike sends yen sinking
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
Warren Buffett VINCENT TULLO FOR WSJ
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Warren Buffett stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. His son Howard succeeds him, effective immediately. Buffett had tipped Howard as Berkshire’s next chairman years earlier. Buffett ceded his role as chief executive to Greg Abel in January. He said he would remain on the board and serve as chairman emeritus.

 

Coinbase climbed about 12%, leading S&P 500 gainers. The crypto exchange said it has sought regulatory approval to list perpetual futures tied to individual large-cap U.S. stocks. The futures, known as perps, are speculative derivative contracts that never expire, allowing traders to pile on leverage that amplifies gains and losses.

 

The yen fell sharply after the Bank of Japan lifted its benchmark interest rate to a 30-year high. The dollar strengthened more than 1% against the yen following the move, a reaction at odds with Tokyo and Washington’s ambitions for a stronger yen. Investors seemingly took issue with dovish signals that sowed doubt how quickly the BOJ will follow through with more rate increases. A dollar bought around 157.8 yen in Asia afternoon trading, compared with the month’s low of 153.54 Sept. 11.

 

An independent security-research team used Anthropic’s Claude software to gain access to an OpenAI employee’s ChatGPT account. The team quickly reported its findings to the company and was participating in a bug-hunting program sponsored by OpenAI. The hack let the researchers read and suggest changes to OpenAI’s cache of software.

 

Major stock-market indexes were mixed. The Nasdaq climbed 0.4%, the S&P 500 advanced 0.2%, and the Dow industrials fell 0.2%. The 10-year Treasury yield rose 4.9 basis points to 4.995%.

One Big Story

 
 
ALEX NABAUM FOR WSJ
 

In their latest incarnations, exchange-traded funds often offer exposure to narrow, risky assets, high tax bills and bloated fees. Many ETFs have become publicly traded gambling chips. Your job as an investor is to resist temptation and to sort through these new offerings without mercy.

 

At least three ETF sponsors have filed to launch funds that would go up or down based on which political party wins upcoming elections. More than 100 proposed ETFs are tied to the real-time success of National Hockey League teams over the course of a season—including 32 that would double the daily change in a composite statistical measure of a team’s performance.

 

There is an old joke that 95% of investing success consists of knowing what not to do. It’s rapidly approaching 99%, and it’s no longer a joke.
